<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||TIDE|947}}</noinclude>coefficient of <math>S_i</math> vanishes. Hence on effecting these substitutions and equating that coefficient to zero, we find
{{block center|<math>-\frac{M}{a^2}e_i+\frac{3ma^2}{2r^3}+\frac{4\pi\sigma a}{2i+1}e_i=0.</math>}}
But by the definitions of <math>\delta</math> and <math>a</math> we have <math>M=\tfrac{4}{3}\pi\delta a^3=ga^2</math>, where <math>g</math> is gravity, and therefore
{{block center|<math>e_i=\frac{\frac{3ma^2}{2gr^3}}{1-\frac{3\sigma}{(2i+1)\delta}}.</math> (6)}}
In the particular case considered in § 11 we therefore have
{{block center|<math>\rho=a\left[1+\frac{3ma^2/2gr^3}{1-3\sigma/5\delta}(\cos^2 z-\tfrac{1}{3})\right]</math> (7)}}
as the equation to the equilibrium tide under the potential
{{block center|<math>V=\frac{3m}{2r^3}\rho^2(\cos^2 z-\tfrac{1}{3}).</math>}}

{{smaller block|If <math>\sigma</math> were very small compared with <math>\delta</math> the attraction of the water on itself would be very small compared with that of the planet on the water; hence we see in the general case that <math>1/\left(1-\frac{3\sigma}{2i+1)\delta}\right)</math> is the factor by which the mutual gravitation of the ocean augments the deformation due to the external forces. This factor will occur frequently hereafter, and therefore for brevity we write
{{block center|<math>b_i=1-\frac{3\sigma}{(2i+1)\delta},</math> (8)}}
and we may put (6) in the form
{{block center|<math>e_i=\frac{3ma^2}{2gr^3b_i}.</math> (9)}}
Comparison with (5) then shows that
{{block center|<math>V=gb_i\left(\frac{\rho}{a}\right)^ie_iS_i</math> (10)}}
is the potential of the disturbing forces under which
{{block center|<math>\rho=a+e_iS_i</math> (11)}}
is a figure of equilibrium.}}

{{smaller block|We are thus provided with a convenient method of specifying any disturbing force by means of the figure of equilibrium which it is competent to maintain. In considering the dynamical theory of the tides on an ocean-covered planet, we shall specify the disturbing forces in the manner expressed by (10) and (11). This way of specifying a disturbing force is equally exact whether or not we choose to include the effects of the mutual attraction of the ocean. If the augmentation due to mutual attraction of the water is not included, <math>b_i</math> becomes equal to unity; there is no longer any necessity to use spherical harmonic analysis, and we see that if the equation to the surface of an ocean be
{{block center|<math>\rho=a+S,</math>}}
where <math>S</math> is a function of latitude and longitude, it is in equilibrium under forces due to a potential whose value at the surface of the sphere (where <math>\rho=a</math>) is <math>gS</math>.}}

{{smaller block|In treating the theory of tidal observation we shall specify the tide-generating forces in this way, and then by means of “the principle of forced vibrations,” referred to in § 7 as used by Laplace for discussing the actual oscillations of the sea, we shall pass to the actual tides at the port of observation.}}

{{smaller block|In this equilibrium theory it is assumed that the figure of the ocean is at each instant one of equilibrium under the action of gravity and
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Effect of Land in Equilibrium Theory.}}
of the tide-generating forces. Lord Kelvin has, however, reasserted<ref>Thomson and Tait, ''Nat. Phil.'' § 807. G. H. Darwin and H. H. Turner, ''Proc. Roy. Soc.'' (1886).</ref> a point which was known to Bernoulli, but has since been overlooked, namely, that this law of rise and fall of water cannot, when portions of the globe are continents, be satisfied by a constant volume of water in the ocean. The necessary correction to the theory depends on the distribution of land and sea, but a numerical solution shows that it is practically of very small amount.}}

{{smaller block|§ 13. ''Development of Tide-generating Potential in Terms of Hour-Angle and Declination.''—We now proceed to develop the tide-generating potential, and shall of course implicitly (§ 12) determine the equation to the equilibrium figure.}}

{{smaller block|We have already seen that, if <math>z</math> be the moon’s zenith distance at the point <math>P</math> on the earth’s surface, whose co-ordinates referred to A, B, C, axes fixed in the earth, and <math>a\xi</math>, <math>a\eta</math>, <math>a\zeta</math>,
{{block center|<math>\cos z=\xi\text{M}_1+\eta\text{M}_2+\zeta\text{M}_3,</math>}}
where <math>\text{M}_1</math>, <math>\text{M}_2</math>, <math>\text{M}_3</math> are the moon’s direction cosines referred to the same axes. Then, with this value of <math>\cos z</math>,
{{block center|<math>\cos^2z-\tfrac{1}{3}=2\xi\eta\text{M}_1\text{M}_2+2\frac{\xi^2-\eta^2}{2}\frac{\text{M}_1^2-\text{M}_2^2}{2}+2\eta\zeta\text{M}_2\text{M}_3+2\xi\zeta\text{M}_1\text{M}_3</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\tfrac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{\xi^2+\eta^2-2\zeta^2}{3}\frac{\text{M}_1^2+\text{M}_2^2-2\text{M}_3^2}{3}.</math> (12)}} The axis of C is taken as the polar axis, and AB is the equatorial plane, so that the functions of <math>\xi</math>, <math>\eta</math>, <math>\zeta</math> are functions of the latitude and longitude of the point <math>P</math>, at which we wish to find the potential.}}

{{smaller block|The functions of <math>\text{M}_1</math>, <math>\text{M}_2</math>, <math>\text{M}_3</math> depend on the moon's position, and we shall have occasion to develop them in two different ways—first in terms of her hour-angle and declination, and secondly (§ 25) in terms of her longitude and the elements of the orbit.}}

{{smaller block|Now let A be on the equator in the meridian of <math>P</math>, and B 90° east of A on the equator. Then, if M be the moon, the inclination of the plane MC to the plane CA is the moon's easterly local hour-angle. Let <math>h_0</math>=Greenwich westward hour-angle; <math>l</math>=the west longitude of the place of observation; <math>\lambda</math>=the latitude of the place; <math>\delta</math>=moon's declination: then we have
{{block center|<math>\text{M}_1 = \cos\delta\cos(h_0-l),\ \text{M}_2 = -\cos\delta\sin(h_0-l),\ \text{M}_3 = \sin\delta,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\xi = \cos\lambda,\ \eta = 0,\ \zeta = \sin\lambda.</math>}}
Also the radius vector of the place of observation on the earth's surface is <math>a</math>. Whence we find
{{block center|<math>V = \frac{3ma^2}{2r^3}\Big\{ \tfrac{1}{2}\cos^2\lambda\cos^2\delta\cos 2(h_0-l) + \sin 2\lambda\,\sin\delta\,\cos\delta\,\cos(h_0-l)</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\tfrac{3}{2}(\tfrac{1}{3}-\sin^2\delta)(\tfrac{1}{3}-\sin^2\lambda)\Big\}</math> (13)}}
The tide-generating forces are found by the rates of variation of <math>V</math> for latitude and longitude, and also for radius <math>a</math>, if we care to find the radial disturbing force.}}

{{smaller block|The westward component of the tide-generating force at the earth's surface, where <math>\rho = a</math>, is <math>dV/a\cos\lambda dl</math>, and the northward component is <math>dV/ad\lambda</math>; the change of apparent level is the ratio of
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|''Potential Developed in Hour-angle and Declination.''}}
these to gravity <math>g</math>. On effecting the differentiations we find that the westward component is made up of two periodic terms, one going through its variations twice and the other once a day. The southward component has also two similar terms; but it has a third very small term, which does not oscillate about a zero value. This last term corresponds to forces which produce a constant heaping up of the water at the equator; or, in other words, the moon's attraction has the effect of causing a small permanent ellipticity of the earth's mean figure. This augmentation of ellipticity is of course very small, but it is necessary to mention it.}}

{{smaller block|If we consider the motion of a pendulum-bob under the influence of these forces during any one day, we see that in consequence of the semi-diurnal changes of level it twice describes an ellipse with major axis east and west, and the formula when developed shows that the ratio of axes is equal to the sine of the latitude, and the linear dimensions proportional to <math>\cos^2\delta</math>. It describes once a day an ellipse whose north and south axis is proportional to <math>\sin 2\delta\cos 2\lambda</math> and whose east and west axis is proportional to <math>\sin 2\delta\sin\lambda</math>. Obviously the latter is circular in latitude 30°. When the moon is on the equator, the maximum deflexion occurs when the moon's local hour-angle is 45°, and is then equal to
{{block center|<math>\frac{3m}{2M}\left(\frac{a}{r}\right)^3\cos\lambda.</math>}}
This angle is equal to 0·0174″ <math>\cos\lambda</math>. Attempts actually to measure the deflexion of the vertical have at length proved successful (see {{sc|Seismometer}}).}}

{{c|III.—{{sc|Dynamical Theory of the Tides}}}}

§ 14. ''Recent Advances in the Dynamical Theory of the Tides.''—The problem of the tidal oscillation of the sea is essentially dynamical. In two papers in the second volume of ''Liouville's Journal'' (1896) H. Poincaré has considered the mathematical principles involved in the problem, where the ocean is interrupted by land as in actuality. He has not sought to obtain numerical results applicable to any given configuration of land and sea, but he has aimed rather at pointing out methods by which it may some day be possible to obtain such solutions.

Even when the ocean is taken as covering the whole earth the problem presents formidable difficulties, and this is the only case in which it has been solved hitherto.<ref>Lord Kelvin's (Sir W. Thomson's) paper on the gravitational oscillations of rotating water, ''Phil. Mag.'' (October 1880), bears on this subject. It is the only attempt to obtain numerical results in respect to the effect of the earth's rotation on the oscillations of land-locked seas.</ref>

Laplace gives the solution in bks. i. and iv. of the ''Mécanique céleste;'' but his work is unnecessarily complicated. In the 9th edition of the ''Ency. Brit.'' we gave Laplace's theory without these complications, but the theory is now accessible in H. Lamb's ''Hydrodynamics'' and other works of the kind. It is therefore not reproduced here.

In 1897 and 1898 S. S. Hough undertook an important revision of Laplace's theory and succeeded not only in introducing the effects of the mutual gravitation of the ocean, but<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
